description: Somos Galactic Thinkers, un grupo de estudiantes de ingeniería de Cajamarca apasionados por la tecnología y la exploración espacial. Combinamos programación, análisis de datos y estudio del terreno para identificar lugares de la Tierra con características similares a la Luna y Marte.
summary:
Órbita is an interactive web platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 to explore, analyze, and compare terrestrial environments that may serve as analogues for the Moon and Mars. The project focuses on identifying geological similarities between planetary landscapes and Earth locations, highlighting Peru's Sechura Desert and Andagua volcanic region while also considering terrestrial analogue environments from other parts of the world.

The platform integrates 3D planetary exploration, interactive maps, terrain visualization, and topographic analysis. Users can explore reference locations such as Jezero Crater on Mars and Shackleton Crater on the Moon, and compare their characteristics with selected terrestrial environments. Its GeoPendiente module provides tools to examine elevation, slope, and terrain morphology, visualize surfaces in 2D and 3D, compare measurements, and export results.

By bringing together planetary reference sites and terrestrial environments from different regions, Órbita helps make scientific terrain analysis more accessible. The project highlights the value of Earth's geological diversity, especially Peru's landscapes, as a resource for planetary research and the preparation of future space exploration missions.

Project Summary

GeoAnálogos Peru is developing Órbita, a web platform for space exploration and geographic analysis that allows you to go from a region of Mars or the Moon to a set of candidate terrains on Earth. The central idea is simple: before proposing a test with a rover, it is advisable to know what slopes, slopes and surfaces each place offers and to what extent these features are close to those of the planetary area that is of interest to study.

The pilot brings together 18 2 × 2 km windows in Peru: nine in Sechura, Piura, associated with Jezero, and nine in Andagua, Arequipa, associated with the Shackleton edge. 20 numerical profiles, including JEZ-01 and SHA-01, are stored in the repository; windows are described as medium slope, proportion of surface with slope less than 8°, robust slope, and coverage. Data are presented as measurements recorded by the project, not as a validated field campaign.

The prototype integrates 3D globes of Earth, Mars, and the Moon; search by names or coordinates; maps with GeoJSON polygons; regional relief meshes; comparison sheets; and a GeoSlope module with grids, contour lines, 2D/3D views, and technical exports. These resources bring topography and planetary exploration closer to the work of Civil Engineering and Systems students.

The main scientific caution is that geometric similarity does not imply equivalent traffic conditions. To convert a sector into an experimental analogue will require data on terrain, roughness, materials, traction, DEM uncertainty and physical conditions of the destination. Consequently, the results of this stage are used to guide questions and pre-select areas, not to certify a test site.

4. Project Details

Executive Summary

Órbita articulates a visual exploration experience with a local geospatial catalog to answer which sectors of Peru can be considered study candidates against specific reliefs of Mars and the Moon. Its contributions focus on the connection between a three-dimensional viewer, an explicit comparison of indicators, and an accessible topographic reading. The repository contains measurements for 18 terrestrial sectors and two references, as well as a coordinate analysis flow that queries external services or imports DEM grids. The advantage of the project is the traceability of the exploration question; its current limitation is the absence in the ZIP of the original rasters, complete production scripts of the 20 measurements, uncertainty logging, and field verification.

1. Project Description

1.1 What it does

Orbit allows you to observe celestial bodies in 3D, recognize craters and regions, alternate optical and relief layers, and access place files. For Peru, it displays a grid of Sechura and Andagua polygons on a Leaflet map, with georeferenced attributes and topographic measurements. The user can also open GeoPendiente to analyze a ground point, represent a grid of elevations, observe curves, and download tables for external workflows.

The catalog's global index compares descriptive profiles of geology, topography, temperature, and environment using exploratory rules. On the other hand, Peruvian sectors do not receive this global index: the application directly presents differences between measured magnitudes. This distinction avoids communicating a percentage of "NASA similarity" that the local calculation does not support.

1.2 How it works

  1. The person chooses Earth, Mars or Moon and uses the globe: rotation, zoom, tilt and search for regions or coordinates.
  2. Select a planetary reference, such as Jezero's environment or Shackleton's edge, and open the comparison view.
  3. The synchronized list and map allow you to filter the nine Peruvian sectors associated with the reference and review the file of a polygon.
  4. The file shows the average slope, smooth surface, slope and coverage available; the differences are absolute and the relative "reading" is only an interpretative order, not an official grade.
  5. From Know Your Terrain, the user can enter WGS84 coordinates or select a sector. The Earth DEM query requires the Internet, or a regular CSV with heights can be imported.
  6. The tool offers 2D/3D outputs, contour lines when a valid grid exists, point files, and PNEZD to Civil 3D export under UTM zone conditions.

Figure 2. Jezero selection and access to the comparator

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

1.3 Innovation and purpose

The innovation is not in proposing that two worlds are identical, but in connecting a spatial selection with an engineering question that can be verified. A plain, a slope or a crater rim are different scenarios for studying navigation. Órbita links these shapes with quantifiable profiles and explains what data is missing to evaluate a specific maneuver.

The combination of planetary globes, regional models, mosaics, polygons, and a survey lab accessible from the same application offers an integrated experience. The use of indicators in physical units and coverage visualization make it easy to discuss the model's limitations rather than hiding them behind a single score.

1.4 Benefits and impact

A. Social, environmental and technological. Remote access helps students and robotics teams identify topics of study before traveling to the field. A more focused visit could reduce preliminary tours, although these savings have not yet been measured.

B. Space missions. The approach is compatible with the preparation of mobility tests: studying a route with slope changes, observing possible relief transitions and formulating operating conditions. It does not replace tensile tests, robotic perception or physically simulated Martian or lunar environments.

C. Impact on the community. The solution can serve as a didactic example to integrate software engineering, cartography, applied mathematics, geotechnics, and topographic representation in the same academic exercise.

1.5 Objectives and expected results

General objective. To develop a web application that compares regions of Mars and the Moon with terrestrial sectors through open geospatial information and topographic analysis, to guide robotic exploration test proposals.

  • Integrate a 3D exploration of the three bodies and link planetary references to regions of the catalog.
  • Identify and georeference 18 terrestrial study windows with polygons and documented centers.
  • Present, with its unit and coverage, indicators of medium slope, smooth surface and local slope.
  • Facilitate land elevation consultation and DEM mesh treatment in 2D/3D views and technical exports.
  • Document provenance, limits, and status of measurements to prepare for independent verification and subsequent testing.

1.6 Methodology and work plan

The work is organized as an iterative process: delimitation of windows, structuring of the catalog, implementation of the viewer, incorporation of indicators, presentation of differences, and review of evidence. The start and end dates per person are not found in the ZIP; for this reason, a progress table is kept without assigning fictitious chronologies.

Spatial criterion. The polygons of Peru are expressed in geographical coordinates of longitude/latitude and are associated with UTM WGS84 zone 17 south (EPSG:32717) for Sechura and zone 18 south (EPSG:32718) for Andagua. Planetary references require their own systems and datums: a terrestrial projection to Mars or the Moon should not be applied directly.

Comparison criterion. In each window, a median slope, the percentage of valid cells with a slope strictly less than 8°, and the slope P95−P5 are considered. To compare magnitudes, absolute differences in degrees, percentage points, and meters are used. The coverage indicates which fraction of the mesh produces a valid slope.

Environmental variables. The world catalog contains descriptive estimates to order candidates; temperatures, winds, pressure, and illumination are not, at this stage, paired and verified observations for the windows of Peru. Therefore, the local reading focuses on topography.

1.7.2 Languages and formats

The application is written primarily in JavaScript and JSX, with React as the interface library, Vite for the development process, and CSS for visual identity. GeoJSON preserves the pilot geometries; JSON registers profiles and rendering meshes; SQL defines a structure for data publishing; and CSV allows georeferenced or local samples to be exchanged. Python appears in the proposed geospatial flow, but ZIP does not provide a complete process for generating each metric with parameters, log, and external reproducibility.

1.7.3 Hardware and Sensors

The interaction requires a browser compatible with modern JavaScript technologies and, for the accelerated 3D globe, WebGL support; the project offers an alternative visualization in Canvas. No physical sensors installed by the team are identified: CTX, LOLA, MODIS, MEDA and Diviner correspond to external scientific platforms. The app consults or presents products derived from these missions and other agencies; it does not take direct readings of the instruments.

1.7.4 Topographic treatment and equations

A digital elevation model (DEM) is a grid that relates planimetric coordinates to heights. To interpret a slope it is necessary to work with separations in meters, known vertical reference, comparable resolution and sufficient coverage. The in-house laboratory calculates gradients with a neighborhood of 3 × 3 (Horn type operator) when it receives a complete grid.

Angular slope: θ = arctan(√[(∂z/∂x)² + (∂z/∂y)²]) × 180/π. Here θ is expressed in degrees; z is elevation in meters, and x and y are horizontal distances in meters.

Percentage slope: i = 100 × √[(∂z/∂x)² + (∂z/∂y)²]. It is essential to distinguish i (%) from θ (°): a slope of 8° does not equal 8%.

Smooth area (%) = (number of valid cells with θ < 8° / number of valid cells) × 100. Coverage (%) = (cells with valid slope / total cells) × 100.

Robust elevation gain (m) = P95(z) − P5(z), where P95 and P5 are the 95th and 5th percentiles of the valid elevations. This indicator reduces the influence of extremes against the maximum–minimum range.

Differences between references: Δθ = |θplanetary − θterrestrial|; ΔA = | Aplanetary − Aterrestrial|, in percentage points; ΔH = | Hplanetary − Hterrestrial|, in meters.

Relative reading on the index cards = | A − B| / max(| A|,| B|) for each indicator; if both are zero, zero is assigned. This criterion helps to order which variable differs more proportionally; it is not a calibrated scientific index of similarity.

Contour lines join points of equal elevation within the same datum and at an equidistance appropriate for the scale. The 2D and 3D surfaces of the laboratory can only be considered quantitative analysis when they come from numerical DEM dimensions; the approximate views are differentiated as illustrations. For Civil 3D, PNEZD points can be exported when the terrestrial grid belongs to a single UTM zone.

From Civil Engineering, the analysis focuses on understanding what a slope means on a surface of different scales, how the slope influences a route and why a 3D representation is not equivalent to a precision topographic survey. It is also essential to differentiate a descriptive classification of orography from the parameters required in a road or geotechnical design. In GeoPendiente the MTC DG-2018 reference is for guidance purposes and does not replace the survey or the regulatory evaluation of a real corridor.

1.10 Impact and benefits

For an eventual robotic mobility campaign, topographic information can help to select test sections that combine smooth surfaces, ramps and altimetry changes. In Civil Engineering, it allows discussion of DEM reading, slopes, profiles, differences between coordinate systems and limits of a vertically exaggerated visualization. In education, it encourages the decision to study a place to be associated with an explicit data, source and uncertainty.

The usefulness does not automatically extend to traffic safety: characteristics such as granulometry, shear resistance, roughness, cohesion, rolling, critical slopes, lighting, gravity, pressure, temperature and radiation require further studies. Nor is the suitability of a track or settlement deduced from a DEM of 100 m.

1.11 Available and expected results

1.11.1 Available Evidence and Status

The terrainMeasurements.json file contains 20 profiles: 18 terrestrial and two planetarium. All windows have a nominal side of 2,000 m, analysis resolution of 100 m, 400 potential cells and a gentle slope threshold of 8° strict. The buildDemo code overlays these measurements on the GeoJSON and assigns a "measured" state, but in the initial GeoJSON "exploratorio_sin_medicion" persists. It is interpreted as a partial update of the catalog and not as evidence of external validation.

The project documentation indicates that the land windows are based on Copernicus DEM GLO-90, with permanent water exclusion using ESA WorldCover; JEZ-01 uses a CTX product, and SHA-01 uses a LOLA Site04 reference. Without the original rasters, reprojection logs, mask, and process scripts, the numbers can be cited as repository data, but not independently recalculated or certified for accuracy.

Martian example. SE-05 has a median slope of 0.2666° compared to 1.9705° in JEZ-01; the difference is 1.7039°. The smooth surface differs by 1.71 percentage points and the robust slope by 11.4036 m. The coverage of the sector is 87.75 %. Although the pair offers comparable variables, it does not represent a validation of mobility: the shape of the microrelief, the ground and the uncertainty still need to be evaluated.

Lunar example. AN-03 has a median slope of 16.0143° compared to 32.1585° in SHA-01; the difference reaches 16.1442°. Its smooth surface is 11%, while SHA-01 registers 0%, and the elevation difference differs 715.6611 m. Therefore, AN-03 is a terrestrial scenario with slopes, but the values of the repository do not support the claim that it faithfully replicates the Shackleton edge.

Selection warning. SE-09 has the smallest difference in median slope compared to JEZ-01 within Sechura, but its coverage is 49.50%. Therefore, it should not be ranked as the best definitive candidate just because a variable is numerically close. The evaluation should apply a justified coverage threshold and review the source, resolution, and intended use.

1.11.3 Functional Verification and Software Results

The npm test command was executed on the ZIP repository and 17 approved tests were obtained, without errors. The tests cover cases of topographic conversion/validation, CSV treatment, PNEZD restrictions, DEM query handling, filtering of Peruvian sectors, and absence of scores when data is missing. This result verifies that the available automated tests are executed correctly; it does not demonstrate by itself the operation of all browsers or scientific validity of the sources.

The terrain-jezero.json and terrain-shackleton.json meshes allow relief to be represented in 96 × 96 visual grids. The Jezero file indicates tile coverage of 80.4% and Shackleton's 100%. These coverages describe the regional display mesh and should not be confused with the 100% assigned to the 2 × 2 km JEZ-01 and SHA-01 windows in terrainMeasurements.json.

1.11.4 Pending validation

  • Attach the original rasters or exact tile identifiers, software, parameters, clipping geometries, and playable intermediate results.
  • Reconcile the "exploratorio_sin_medicion" field of GeoJSON with the "measured" state assigned by the catalog construction and publish acceptance criteria.
  • Apply cell coverage and quality controls before making conclusions on SE-07, SE-08 and SE-09.
  • Document vertical/horizontal uncertainty, missing data processing, resolution effect, and 8° threshold sensitivity.
  • Record a demonstration and representative test on the published version; any physical test must have its own plan and protocol.

1.12 Conclusions and future improvements

First conclusion. There is an integrated application and an initial set of 18 Peruvian study sectors associated with two planetary references. The code allows you to travel through the regions and consult topographic information in an organized manner, which satisfies the objective of an educational and exploratory prototype.

Second conclusion. The repository offers specific numerical measurements that allow comparing magnitudes with units and coverage. In Sechura medium-low slopes predominate, but there are sectors with very small fractions of valid data; in Andagua a more pronounced relief is recorded. The contrast with Jezero and Shackleton shows differences, not a scientific homologation of terrain.

Third conclusion. The integration of GeoPendiente brings specific value to Civil Engineering: DEM reading, gradient calculation, curve representation, UTM/WGS84 systems and point preparation for topographic software. However, a freely accessible DEM dimension does not replace a field survey or authorize structural or road design decisions.

Future improvements. Publish the reproducible flow of computation and raster data; define coverage thresholds and uncertainty bands; add field validation and mechanical properties of the soil; review the temporal and spatial correspondence of environmental variables; expand planetary cases; and document robotic tests linked to a specific procedure.

Learning design. The greatest methodological contribution was to turn a visual exploration into a file of reasoned decisions. The next step should be to back up that file with sufficient data quality and traceability for another person to repeat the operations.

1.13 Annexes and appendices

The annexes are incorporated at the end of the document to preserve the main body in a legible way: Annex A (geometries and metrics), Annex B (procedure and code), Annex C (responsibilities), Annex D (visual evidence) and Annex E (validation checklist). The spaces for images are editable and are located next to the section that justifies.

5. Use of artificial intelligence

According to the statement included in the original document, ChatGPT was used as a support to order and write the documentation and explore visual proposals. This report was also prepared from the files provided and document consistency checks. The responsibility for contrasting sources, validating spatial data, reviewing values and approving conclusions rests with the team.

No further development, image production, video editing, or calculations are attributed to other AI tools because no supported statement was found in the reviewed files. If used, record tool, specific task, approximate date, and human review performed.

6. Data from NASA and other programs

The project uses or cites resources from various institutions. The primary ground elevation product declared in the code is Copernicus DEM GLO-90 (ESA/Copernicus), not a NASADEM product. The original document mentioned NASADEM as the intended source; it is retained here as a planning reference, but the values in the table are not attributed to NASADEM when the software catalogue identifies Copernicus.

7. Space Agency Partners and Other Programs

The project is presented within the framework of the NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026. Appendices

Appendix A. Exploratory grid and geographic traceability

The src/data/sectors.geojson file contains 18 Polygon geometries, each with a design area of 4 km². The nine windows of Sechura are documented in EPSG:32717 and the nine of Andagua in EPSG:32718 for metric analysis, while GeoJSON expresses vertices as [longitude, latitude] in geographic coordinates. The sector identifier allows each polygon to be linked to terrainMeasurements.json. Tables 1 and 2 contain the 18 complete profiles.

Control state: GeoJSON maintains numeric values in null and marks the sectors as "exploratorio_sin_medicion"; buildDemo incorporates JSON values from metrics and publishes the "measured" status in the local catalog. Before a scientific delivery, it is recommended to unify both representations and indicate a date, algorithm and review per record.

Annex B. Proposed reproducible technical flow

  1. To delimit an exactly equivalent window in both bodies and to record their coordinates, projection, datum and extension in meters.
  2. Download the official DEM product and document identifier, native resolution, date or version, and restrictions on use.
  3. Apply a cell mask without data and, on Earth, document the permanent water exclusion criteria.
  4. Redesign and resample both windows in a 100 m mesh using an explicit method; save the interpolation and its parameters.
  5. Calculate median slope, soft fraction less than 8°, P95–P5, total cells and coverage; contrast with other software.
  6. Save an auditable table by sector with values, units, spatial system, source and calculation version.
  7. Examine differences and limits of the robotic assay; reject or mark as preliminary a comparison with insufficient coverage.

Clarification. This flow is proposed as an audit protocol. The ZIP contains functions for querying and analysis in the interface, but it does not include a complete package of rasters and scripts that allows the 20 stored profiles to be replayed from start to finish.
